claims.evidence: This is based on cryo-EM data analysis.

claims.claim: For all actin isoforms, the highest local resolutions were obtained in the central core region.
claims.source: For all actin isoforms, the highest local resolutions were obtained in the central core region.
claims.evidence: This is based on cryo-EM data analysis.

claims.claim: Lower local resolutions were obtained in the most surface-exposed and flexible regions such as the N-terminus and the D-loop.
claims.source: Lower local resolutions were obtained in the most surface-exposed and flexible regions such as the N-terminus and the D-loop as expected.
claims.evidence: This is based on cryo-EM data analysis and is consistent with expectations.

claims.claim: All actin structures were solved in the Mg2+·ADP state.
claims.source: All actin structures were solved in the Mg2+·ADP state (Figure 1E, Figure 2) and have been obtained without the use of stabilizing drugs that may interfere with the filament structure (Diensthuber et al., 2011; Isambert et al., 1995; Zimmermann et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This describes the nucleotide state of the structures.

claims.claim: The actin structures have been obtained without the use of stabilizing drugs that may interfere with the filament structure.
claims.source: All actin structures were solved in the Mg2+·ADP state (Figure 1E, Figure 2) and have been obtained without the use of stabilizing drugs that may interfere with the filament structure (Diensthuber et al., 2011; Isambert et al., 1995; Zimmermann et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental conditions and is supported by citations.

claims.claim: The superposition of all actin isoform structures shows a root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) between 0.83Å to 1.04Å for Cα atoms, indicating an overall similar topology.
claims.source: The superposition of all actin isoform structures shows a root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) between 0.83Å to 1.04Å for Cα atoms, indicating an overall similar topology.
claims.evidence: This is based on structural comparison analysis.

claims.claim: No significant differences in the pitch of the actin helix were observed between structures of actin isoforms.
claims.source: No significant differences in the pitch of the actin helix were observed between our structures of actin isoforms, emphasizing their overall conserved filamentous structure in the absence of myosin motors or ABPs.
claims.evidence: This is based on structural analysis.

claims.claim: Actin isoforms show the largest divergence at the acidic N-terminus within SD1.
claims.source: Actin isoforms show the largest divergence at the acidic N-terminus within SD1 (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is based on sequence and structural analysis.

claims.claim: There are no substitutions in SD2, the smallest and most flexible subdomain.
claims.source: There are no substitutions in SD2, the smallest and most flexible subdomain (Kudryashov and Reisler, 2013).
claims.evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and is supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The nucleotide-binding cleft active site is conserved between actin isoforms.
claims.source: Our cryo-EM reconstructions show that the nucleotide-binding cleft active site is conserved between actin isoforms (Figure 1E and Figure 2).
claims.evidence: This is based on structural analysis.

claims.claim: The densities for Mg2+ and ADP were assigned without ambiguity.
claims.source: The densities for Mg2+ and ADP were assigned without ambiguity and revealed interactions with amino acids located in SD2 (Q58/Q59 and Y68/Y69) and SD4 (E206/E207, R209/R210, K212/K213, and E213/E214) but also with amino acids located in SD1 (M15/L16, K17/K18, Q136/Q137, and Y336/Y337) and SD3 (D156/D157, M304/M305, Y305/Y306, and K335/K336; Figure 2).
claims.evidence: This is based on cryo-EM density analysis.

claims.claim: Amino acid Y305/Y306 forms π-π interactions with the adenine ring of ADP.
claims.source: While most of the interactions are polar and electrostatic, amino acid Y305/Y306 forms π-π interactions with the adenine ring of ADP.
claims.evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the active site.

claims.claim: The superimposition of the nucleotide cleft active sites of the four structures of actin isoforms shows small differences in the positions of the nucleotide (RMSD ~0.44–0.47 Å).
claims.source: The superimposition of the nucleotide cleft active sites of our four structures of actin isoforms shows small differences in the positions of the nucleotide (RMSD ~0.44–0.47 Å) and the bound Mg2+ (RMSD ~0.5–1.3 Å), especially in the position of the β-phosphate group relative to the α-phosphate group (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claims.claim: The superimposition of the nucleotide cleft active sites shows small differences in the positions of the bound Mg2+ (RMSD ~0.5–1.3 Å).
claims.source: The superimposition of the nucleotide cleft active sites of our four structures of actin isoforms shows small differences in the positions of the nucleotide (RMSD ~0.44–0.47 Å) and the bound Mg2+ (RMSD ~0.5–1.3 Å), especially in the position of the β-phosphate group relative to the α-phosphate group (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claims.claim: Amino acid substitution M15/L16 between nonmuscle and muscle actin does not alter the overall topology of the nucleotide-binding site.
claims.source: Amino acid substitution M15/L16 between nonmuscle and muscle actin does not alter the overall topology of the nucleotide-binding site.
claims.evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claims.claim: The longer side chain of M15 in nonmuscle actins acts as an extended lid that flanks the active site and shields the phosphate groups of ADP.
claims.source: Instead, the longer side chain of M15 in nonmuscle actins, located in a loop that protrudes into the nucleotide-binding cleft, acts as an extended lid that flanks the active site and shields the phosphate groups of ADP (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on structural analysis.

claims.claim: Amino acids C10 and V17 in muscle actins are substituted with V9/I9 and C16 in β/γ-actin.
claims.source: Near the nucleotide-binding cleft active site, amino acids C10 and V17 in muscle actins are substituted with V9/I9 and C16 in β/γ-actin (Figure 3, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is based on sequence and structural analysis.

claims.claim: Reciprocal amino acid substitutions C10/V17 and V9/I9/C16 maintain the overall oxidation-reduction environment within filamentous actin isoforms.
claims.source: These reciprocal amino acid substitutions maintain the overall oxidation-reduction environment within filamentous actin isoforms which is important for its dynamic properties and the interaction with some regulatory proteins (Farah et al., 2011; Lassing et al., 2007; Wilson et al., 2016; Terman and Kashina, 2013).
claims.evidence: This is based on structural analysis and is supported by citations.

claims.claim: Longitudinal interactions are mainly mediated by hydrophilic amino acids that are likely to enable interactions with water molecules.
claims.source: The analysis of interprotomer interfaces in our four structures of actin isoforms (Figure 4, Figure 5, Figure 4—figure supplement 1) showed that longitudinal interactions are mainly mediated by hydrophilic amino acids that are likely to enable interactions with water molecules that were recently shown to mediate interprotomer contacts within the filament core (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Reynolds et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This is based on structural analysis and is supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Amino acid substitutions at the longitudinal interprotomer interface include L175/M176, T200/V201, Q224/N225, C271/A272, F278/Y279, and V286/I287.
claims.source: Amino acid substitutions at the longitudinal interprotomer interface (also called long pitch helix interface) include L175/M176, T200/V201, Q224/N225, C271/A272, F278/Y279, and V286/I287.
claims.evidence: This is based on structural analysis.

claims.claim: The transverse interprotomer interface is formed through hydrophilic and hydrophobic interactions.
claims.source: The transverse interprotomer interface (also called short pitch helix interface) is formed through hydrophilic and hydrophobic interactions (Figure 5, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on structural analysis.

claims.claim: Most of the transverse interprotomer interactions are direct and not mediated by solvent.
claims.source: In contrast to interactions at the longitudinal interface, most of the transverse interprotomer interactions are direct and not mediated by solvent.
claims.evidence: This is based on structural analysis.

claims.claim: A single amino acid substitution (V286/I287) is present at the transverse interprotomer interface.
claims.source: A single amino acid substitution (V286/I287) is present at the transverse interprotomer interface.
claims.evidence: This is based on structural analysis.

claims.claim: Amino acid I287 is in hydrophobic contact with I208 and L242 in muscle actins and buries a surface area of ~113 Å2.
claims.source: Amino acid I287 is in hydrophobic contact with I208 and L242 in muscle actins and buries a surface area of ~113 Å2, whereas the interaction between V286, I207, and L241 in nonmuscle actins is less hydrophobic and buries a surface area of ~83 Å2 in the transverse interprotomer interface (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D).
claims.evidence: This is based on structural analysis.

claims.claim: The interaction between V286, I207, and L241 in nonmuscle actins is less hydrophobic and buries a surface area of ~83 Å2 in the transverse interprotomer interface.
claims.source: Amino acid I287 is in hydrophobic contact with I208 and L242 in muscle actins and buries a surface area of ~113 Å2, whereas the interaction between V286, I207, and L241 in nonmuscle actins is less hydrophobic and buries a surface area of ~83 Å2 in the transverse interprotomer interface (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D).
claims.evidence: This is based on structural analysis.

claims.claim: Interactions with the D-loop located in SD2 are conserved in structures of actin isoforms.
claims.source: Interactions with the D-loop located in SD2 are conserved in our structures of actin isoforms, underlining the critical and conserved role of the D-loop to mediate interprotomer interactions.
claims.evidence: This is based on structural analysis.

claims.claim: At the intersection of the longitudinal and transverse interprotomer interfaces, H39/40 and H172/H173 together with M43/M44 act as central anchors.
claims.source: At the intersection of the longitudinal and transverse interprotomer interfaces, H39/40 and H172/H173 together with M43/M44 act as central anchors.
claims.evidence: This is based on structural analysis.

claims.claim: The quality of the density maps allowed resolution of both key PTMs (Nt-acetylation and H72/H73 methylation).
claims.source: The quality of our density maps allowed us to resolve both key PTMs (Figure 1E, Figure 1—video 5, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is based on cryo-EM data analysis.

claims.claim: The presence of resolvable density allowed modeling of the entire N-terminus including the Nt-acetylated D1 (D1Ac) and the Nt-acetylated E1 (E1Ac) in the cryo-EM reconstructions of β- and γ-actin.
claims.source: Specifically, the presence of resolvable density allowed us to model the entire N-terminus including the Nt-acetylated D1 (D1Ac) and the Nt-acetylated E1 (E1Ac) in the cryo-EM reconstructions of β- and γ-actin (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: This is based on cryo-EM data analysis.

claims.claim: The acetylation site on the N-terminus is exposed on the filament surface and adds an additional negative charge to the already negatively charged N-terminus.
claims.source: The acetylation site on the N-terminus is exposed on the filament surface and adds an additional negative charge to the already negatively charged N-terminus (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is based on structural analysis and chemical properties.

claims.claim: There are no resolvable densities for the very N-terminus, including Nt-acetylation, in density maps of skeletal muscle α-actin and cardiac muscle α-actin.
claims.source: Like in previous cryo-EM structures of muscle α-actins, there are no resolvable densities for the very N-terminus, including Nt-acetylation, in our density maps of skeletal muscle α-actin and cardiac muscle α-actin (Figure 1E), possibly due to nonuniform PTM patterns of native, tissue-purified muscle actins.
claims.evidence: This is based on cryo-EM data analysis and comparison with previous structures.

claims.claim: The methylated H72/H73 (H72Me/H73Me) was resolved in all cryo-EM reconstructions of actin isoforms.
claims.source: In addition to Nt-acetylation in β- and γ-actin, we could resolve the methylated H72/H73 (H72Me/H73Me) in all cryo-EM reconstructions of actin isoforms (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is based on cryo-EM data analysis.

claims.claim: The presence of both key PTMs in the cryo-EM reconstructions emphasizes that recombinant human actins represent bona fide post-translationally processed, mature nonmuscle actins.
claims.source: The presence of both key PTMs in our cryo-EM reconstructions emphasizes that our recombinant human actins represent bona fide post-translationally processed, mature nonmuscle actins (Hatano et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is based on the structural data and is supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Myosin motors bind actin in a nucleotide-dependent, reversible manner to generate force and motion.
claims.source: Myosin motors bind actin in a nucleotide-dependent, reversible manner to generate force and motion (Heissler and Sellers, 2016a; Sellers, 2000).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: The myosin enzymatic cycle can be categorized into states with weak (ATP and ADP·Pi) and strong (ADP and nucleotide-free [rigor]) actin affinity.
claims.source: The myosin enzymatic cycle can be categorized into states with weak (ATP and ADP·Pi) and strong (ADP and nucleotide-free [rigor]) actin affinity (De La Cruz and Ostap, 2009; Heissler and Sellers, 2016b).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: In the strong affinity states, a binding interface is established between actin and the myosin motor domain.
claims.source: In the strong affinity states, a binding interface is established between actin and the myosin motor domain (von der Ecken et al., 2016; Doran and Lehman, 2021; Lorenz and Holmes, 2010).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Myosin binding to actin filaments causes subtle conformational changes in the filament.
claims.source: Myosin binding to actin filaments causes subtle conformational changes in the filament (Figure 6).
claims.evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claims.claim: Superimposition of the actin structures showed that the Cα of bare and myosin-bound actin protomers deviate with an RMSD of ~1.25–3 Å.
claims.source: Superimposition of the actin structures showed that the Cα of bare and myosin-bound actin protomers deviate with an RMSD of ~1.25–3 Å.
claims.evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claims.claim: The conformational changes in actin upon myosin binding are similar for myosins from different classes and independent of the nucleotide state of the respective motor domain.
claims.source: These changes are similar for myosins from different classes and independent of the nucleotide state of the respective motor domain (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claims.claim: SD2 adopts a different conformation in myosin-bound actin compared to bare actin.
claims.source: The superposition of structures of bare actin isoforms and known structures of myosin-bound actins shows that SD2 adopts a different conformation (Figure 6A and B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1, Figure 6—video 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claims.claim: The conformation of the D-loop differs with a Cα RMSD of ~0.95–1.25 Å between bare and myosin-bound actin.
claims.source: The conformation of the D-loop, located in SD2, differs with a Cα RMSD of ~0.95–1.25 Å (Figure 6A and B).
claims.evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claims.claim: Superimposition of bare γ-actin with γ-actin/NM2C complex shows the subtle inward movement of the D-loop with a Cα RMSD of ~1.25 Å in the myosin-bound state.
claims.source: Superimposition of bare γ-actin with γ-actin/NM2C complex shows the subtle inward movement of the D-loop with a Cα RMSD of ~1.25 Å in the myosin-bound state, suggesting that myosin-binding induces subtle changes in the barbed end groove that do not change the separation between SD1/SD3 and SD2/SD4.
claims.evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claims.claim: The inward movement of the D-loop (RMSD ~0.91 Å) is also observed in the structure of cardiac myosin bound to the thin filament compared to the structure of bare cardiac muscle α-actin.
claims.source: The inward movement of the D-loop (RMSD ~0.91 Å) is also observed in the recent structure of cardiac myosin bound to the thin filament compared to our structure of bare cardiac muscle α-actin (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), suggesting that myosin and not the regulatory proteins tropomyosin and troponin drive this structural change.
claims.evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claims.claim: The D-loop conformation does not change significantly with respect to the nucleotide states (rigor versus ADP) of the compared myosins.
claims.source: The analysis of the actomyosin interface also shows that the D-loop conformation does not change significantly with respect to the nucleotide states (rigor versus ADP) of the compared myosins (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claims.claim: The superimposition of bare and myosin-bound actin structures shows that the N-termini of skeletal muscle α-actin points in a different direction compared to those from ß-actin and γ-actin.
claims.source: The superimposition of bare and myosin-bound actin structures shows that the N-termini of skeletal muscle α-actin points in a different direction compared to those from ß-actin and γ-actin (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claims.claim: The actin N-terminus is positioned closer to the filament surface in myosin-bound structures compared to bare actin structures.
claims.source: The actin N-terminus is positioned closer to the filament surface in myosin-bound structures compared to our bare actin structures (Figure 7, Figure 6—video 1, Figure 7—video 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claims.claim: The negatively charged N-termini of bare ß-actin and γ-actin are near loop-2, a major element of the actomyosin interface that is rich in positively charged amino acids and variable in length.
claims.source: The negatively charged N-termini of bare ß-actin and γ-actin are near loop-2, a major element of the actomyosin interface that is rich in positively charged amino acids and variable in length (Heissler and Manstein, 2011; Joel et al., 2001; Murphy and Spudich, 1999; Uyeda et al., 1994).
claims.evidence: This is based on structural analysis and is supported by citations.

claims.claim: The interface between the actin N-terminus and myosin loop-2 is likely to represent one of the initial contact sites upon the formation of a transient intermediate between both proteins during the formation of the actomyosin complex.
claims.source: This interface is likely to represent one of the initial contact sites upon the formation of a transient intermediate between both proteins during the formation of the actomyosin complex.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on structural analysis.

claims.claim: Nt-acetylation of actin likely enhances long-range electrostatic interactions between actin and myosin that subsequently trigger allosteric structural changes.
claims.source: Nt-acetylation of actin likely enhances long-range electrostatic interactions between both proteins that subsequently trigger allosteric structural changes that result in the formation of the actomyosin interface as suggested previously (Abe et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on structural analysis and is supported by a citation.

claims.claim: A cluster of positively charged amino acids (R661, R663, and R664) in loop-2 of NM2C may interact with either the acetylated N-terminus of ß-actin (D1Ac, D2, and D3) or the acetylated N-terminus of γ-actin (E1Ac, E2, and E3) to stabilize the interface.
claims.source: Furthermore, we observed a cluster of positively charged amino acids (R661, R663, and R664) in loop-2 of NM2C that may interact with either the acetylated N-terminus of ß-actin (D1Ac, D2, and D3) or the acetylated N-terminus of γ-actin (E1Ac, E2, and E3; Figure 7B–C) to stabilize the interface.
claims.evidence: This is based on structural analysis.

claims.claim: A shorter loop-2, as it is found in M1B, is less efficient in stabilizing the actin N-terminus due to geometric constraints that limit its ability to pull the N-terminus closer to the filament surface in the strong binding states compared to a longer loop-2 as it is found in NM2C.
claims.source: We also showed that a shorter loop-2, as it is found in M1B, is less efficient in stabilizing the actin N-terminus due to geometric constraints that limit its ability to pull the N-terminus closer to the filament surface in the strong binding states compared to a longer loop-2 as it is found in NM2C (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claims.claim: Distinct actin-myosin interfaces are formed between actin isoforms and myosin motor proteins that may determine the strength of the interaction and biochemical outputs.
claims.source: This suggests that distinct actin-myosin interfaces are formed between actin isoforms and myosin motor proteins that may determine the strength of the interaction and biochemical outputs.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on structural analysis.

claims.claim: The overall structure of actin isoforms is conserved, as expected from the high-sequence conservation.
claims.source: The overall structure of actin isoforms is conserved, as expected from the high-sequence conservation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on structural analysis and sequence comparison.

claims.claim: Minor differences were observed near the nucleotide-binding cleft that may contribute to the reported differences in the biochemistries of actin isoforms.
claims.source: However, each structure shows subtle but defining differences. Minor differences were observed near the nucleotide-binding cleft (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) that may contribute to the reported differences in the biochemistries of actin isoforms (Chen et al., 2021; Bergeron et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is based on structural analysis and is supported by citations.

claims.claim: The transverse interface is more conserved compared to the longitudinal interprotomer interface.
claims.source: The comparison of longitudinal and transverse interprotomer interfaces revealed that the transverse interface is, with only one amino acid substitution (V286/I287), more conserved compared to the longitudinal interprotomer interface which features several amino acid substitutions (L175/M176, T200/V201, Q224/N225, C271/A272, F278/Y279, and V286/I287; Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and D, Figure 5).
claims.evidence: This is based on structural analysis.

claims.claim: Conserved amino acids (H39/H40, H172/H173, and M43/M44) at the intersection of the longitudinal and transverse interprotomer interfaces are highly susceptible to oxidative stress caused by reactive oxygen species.
claims.source: These residues were previously shown to be highly susceptible to oxidative stress caused by reactive oxygen species and suggest a possible implication for the filament stability of actin isoforms (Varland et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The absence of amino acid substitutions in SD2 and conserved interactions between the SD2 D-loop and amino acids of SD1 and SD3 suggests selective pressure to maintain this critical structural element.
claims.source: The absence of amino acid substitutions in SD2 and conserved interactions between the SD2 D-loop and amino acids of SD1 and SD3 suggests selective pressure to maintain this critical structural element.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on structural analysis.

claims.claim: The D-loop of actin isoforms is located closer to the filament surface in myosin-bound structures compared to structures of bare actin filaments.
claims.source: We also noticed that the D-loop of actin isoforms is located closer to the filament surface in myosin-bound structures compared to structures of bare actin filaments.
claims.evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claims.claim: The most prominent structural change between bare actin isoforms corresponds to the N-terminus location.
claims.source: The most prominent structural change between bare actin isoforms corresponds to the N-terminus location (Figure 1, Figure 7).
claims.evidence: This is based on structural analysis.

claims.claim: The different conformations of the N-terminus between muscle and nonmuscle actins contribute to the formation of actin isoform-specific interfaces with myosin motors involving a more subtle movement of the N-terminus rather than a large-scale pulling mechanism.
claims.source: Based on our structures that show different conformations of the N-terminus between muscle and nonmuscle actins, we suggest that instead of a large conformational change through a pulling mechanism, actin isoform-specific interfaces with myosin motors are formed that involve a more subtle movement of the N-terminus.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on structural comparison.

claims.claim: Different interfaces between actin isoforms and myosin motors together with the subtle differences in the amino acid sequence of the N-terminus region are likely to contribute to the extent actin isoforms can activate the enzyme function of myosin motors in vitro and in cells.
claims.source: These different interfaces together with the subtle differences in the amino acid sequence of the N-terminus region are likely to contribute to the extent actin isoforms can activate the enzyme function of myosin motors in vitro and in cells (Müller et al., 2013; Lappalainen, 2016).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on structural analysis and is supported by citations.

claims.claim: Most cells maintain multiple actin isoforms and a defined complement of myosin motors.
claims.source: In fact, most cells maintain multiple actin isoforms and a defined complement of myosin motors (Kashina, 2020; Otey et al., 1987; Sellers, 2000; Heissler and Sellers, 2016b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations.

claims.claim: Cell type-specific mixing and matching of actin isoforms and myosin motors is likely to fine-tune the enzymatic output of myosin motors for specialized functions.
claims.source: This cell type-specific mixing and matching is likely to fine-tune the enzymatic output of myosin motors for specialized functions (Kee et al., 2009; Müller et al., 2013; Sun et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is an inference supported by citations.

claims.claim: Previous in vitro experiments with recombinant proteins revealed isoform-specific differences in the interaction between muscle and nonmuscle actin isoforms and individual myosin motors.
claims.source: For example, previous in vitro experiments with recombinant proteins revealed isoform-specific differences in the interaction between muscle and nonmuscle actin isoforms and individual myosin motors (Müller et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Predominantly nonsarcomeric myosins have a faster ATPase activity and in vitro sliding velocity when assayed with nonmuscle actins compared to muscle actin.
claims.source: Notably, predominantly nonsarcomeric myosins have a faster ATPase activity and in vitro sliding velocity when assayed with nonmuscle actins compared to muscle actin, suggesting selective fine-tuning of the functional competencies of myosin-actin combinations with implications for cell function (Müller et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The biochemical properties of the very N-terminus of actin isoforms are key contributors to the formation of isoform-specific interfaces with myosin motors.
claims.source: Based on our structural and previous biochemical studies, we speculate that the biochemical properties of the very N-terminus of actin isoforms are key contributors to the formation of isoform-specific interfaces with myosin motors (Müller et al., 2013; Cook et al., 1993; Abe et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on structural analysis and is supported by citations.

claims.claim: The very N-termini of mature β-actin (DDD) and γ-actin (EEE) have different pKa values, resulting in a higher negative electron charge density in β-actin compared to γ-actin.
claims.source: For instance, the very N-termini of mature β-actin (DDD) and γ-actin (EEE) have different pKa values, resulting in a higher negative electron charge density in β-actin compared to γ-actin that is further increased by Nt-acetylation in both isoforms.
claims.evidence: This is based on chemical properties and structural analysis.

claims.claim: Differences in charge density at the N-terminus are likely to contribute to distinct interactions with the positively charged loop-2 and other actin-binding elements in the motor domain of myosin family members during the formation of the actomyosin interface.
claims.source: These differences are likely to contribute to distinct interactions with the positively charged loop-2 and other actin-binding elements in the motor domain of myosin family members during the formation of the actomyosin interface.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on structural and chemical analysis.

claims.claim: Actin isoform-specific interfaces may be further diversified by differential N-terminal processing of β-actin, PTMs, and alternatively spliced myosin motors.
claims.source: Actin isoform-specific interfaces may be further diversified by differential N-terminal processing of β-actin, PTMs, and alternatively spliced myosin motors (Varland et al., 2019; Müller et al., 2013; Arnesen et al., 2018; Terman and Kashina, 2013; Heissler and Manstein, 2011; Sheff and Rubenstein, 1989; Solomon and Rubenstein, 1985).
claims.evidence: This is speculation supported by citations.

claims.claim: The Nt-acetylated N-termini of actin isoforms would likely be more efficient to establish electrostatic interactions with the positively charged loop-2 of myosin.
claims.source: For example, the Nt-acetylated N-termini of actin isoforms would likely be more efficient to establish electrostatic interactions with the positively charged loop-2 of myosin, while the addition of a positive charge to the N-terminus of β-actin through arginylation may weaken the interaction.
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on chemical properties.

claims.claim: The addition of a positive charge to the N-terminus of β-actin through arginylation may weaken the interaction with myosin.
claims.source: For example, the Nt-acetylated N-termini of actin isoforms would likely be more efficient to establish electrostatic interactions with the positively charged loop-2 of myosin, while the addition of a positive charge to the N-terminus of β-actin through arginylation may weaken the interaction.
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on chemical properties.

claims.claim: The actin N-terminus has been shown previously to interact with numerous ABPs.
claims.source: While we focused our comparative structural analysis on the interaction between actin isoforms with myosin motors, the actin N-terminus has been shown previously to interact with numerous ABPs (Arnesen et al., 2018; Cook et al., 1993; Abe et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations.

claims.claim: The proposed isoform-specific interaction mechanisms that stem from the different conformations of the N-termini extend to ABPs.
claims.source: Therefore, we speculate that the proposed isoform-specific interaction mechanisms that stem from the different conformations of the N-termini extend to ABPs.
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on structural analysis.

claims.claim: The structures of single-isotype, post-translationally modified bare skeletal muscle α-actin, cardiac muscle α-actin, ß-actin, and γ-actin reveal general principles, similarities, and differences between isoforms.
claims.source: Collectively, the structures of single-isotype, post-translationally modified bare skeletal muscle α-actin, cardiac muscle α-actin, ß-actin, and γ-actin reveal general principles, similarities, and differences between isoforms.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the structural findings.

claims.claim: The structures complement the repertoire of known actin structures and allow for a comprehensive understanding of in vitro and in vivo functions of actin isoforms.
claims.source: They complement the repertoire of known actin structures and allow for a comprehensive understanding of in vitro and in vivo functions of actin isoforms.
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement about the contribution of the work.

claims.claim: Rabbit skeletal muscle α-actin (UniProt ID: P68135) was prepared from acetone powder.
claims.source: Rabbit skeletal muscle α-actin (UniProt ID: P68135) was prepared from acetone powder (Pel-Freez Biologicals, Rogers, AR, USA) as described earlier (Heissler et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental method.

results.result: High-resolution cryo-EM structures of four actin isoforms (skeletal muscle α-actin at 3.37 Å, cardiac muscle α-actin at 3.07 Å, β-actin at 2.99 Å, and γ-actin at 3.38 Å) were determined in the Mg2+·ADP state without stabilizing drugs, with local resolutions ranging from 1.5-4.4 Å and highest resolution in the core region.
results.evaluation: Claims C1 and C22-C29 collectively describe the structural determination with specific resolution values, nucleotide state, and quality metrics. The data is supported by cryo-EM density maps (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 2), FSC curves, and detailed methods. The resolution values and local resolution distributions are consistent with high-quality cryo-EM reconstructions.

results.result: The structures revealed isoform-specific conformations of the N-terminus, with the N-termini of muscle and nonmuscle actins having different orientations. The N-terminus shifts closer to the filament surface upon myosin binding, establishing isoform-specific interfaces.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C3, C21, C32, C69, C70, and C83 describe the key structural finding regarding N-terminal conformations. This is supported by structural data (Figures 1, 3, 7) showing different N-terminal positions in bare actin isoforms and comparison with myosin-bound structures. The structural evidence directly demonstrates these conformational differences.

results.result: Post-translational modifications (Nt-acetylation and H72/H73 methylation) were resolved in the cryo-EM structures. The entire N-terminus including Nt-acetylated D1 and E1 was modeled in β- and γ-actin, while muscle actins showed incomplete N-terminal density, possibly due to nonuniform PTM patterns in native preparations.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C57 and C115-C121 describe the resolution of PTMs and N-terminal regions. This is supported by cryo-EM density maps (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 3) showing clear density for acetylation and methylation sites. The differential resolution between recombinant (uniform PTM) and native (potentially heterogeneous PTM) actins provides a reasonable explanation for the observed differences.

results.result: The overall structure of actin isoforms is highly conserved, with RMSD between 0.83-1.04 Å for Cα atoms, characteristic double-stranded helical structure (helical rise ~27.6-28 Å, twist ~-166.5° to -168°), and no significant differences in helix pitch.
results.evaluation: Claims C30, C31, C77, and C114 describe the overall structural conservation. This is supported by structural superposition analysis and comparison with previous structures. The RMSD values and helical parameters are consistent with high sequence conservation (~93-99% identity) and previous cryo-EM studies cited in the manuscript.

results.result: The nucleotide-binding cleft active site is conserved between actin isoforms, with Mg2+ and ADP densities assigned unambiguously. Small differences in nucleotide and Mg2+ positions (RMSD ~0.44-1.3 Å) were observed. The M15/L16 substitution does not alter overall topology but M15 in nonmuscle actins acts as an extended lid shielding the phosphate groups.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C40 describe the nucleotide-binding site structure and conservation. This is supported by high-resolution cryo-EM density (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) showing clear density for Mg2+, ADP, and coordinating residues. The structural comparison and RMSD values are appropriate for the reported resolution. The interpretation of M15 as an extended lid is supported by structural data.

results.result: Reciprocal amino acid substitutions (C10/V17 in muscle actins and V9/I9/C16 in β/γ-actin) maintain the overall oxidation-reduction environment within filamentous actin isoforms.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C42 describe reciprocal cysteine substitutions and their functional implications. The structural observation is supported by sequence analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) and structural data (Figure 3). The interpretation regarding oxidation-reduction environment is supported by citations to previous work on actin redox regulation.

results.result: Analysis of interprotomer interfaces revealed that longitudinal interactions are mainly mediated by hydrophilic amino acids (with substitutions L175/M176, T200/V201, Q224/N225, C271/A272, F278/Y279, V286/I287), while the transverse interface is more conserved with only one substitution (V286/I287) and features direct hydrophobic interactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C49 and C79 describe interprotomer interface characteristics. This is supported by structural analysis (Figures 4, 5, Figure 4—figure supplement 1) showing interface residues and buried surface area calculations. The distinction between water-mediated longitudinal and direct transverse interactions is supported by structural data and citation to recent work on water-mediated contacts.

results.result: The D-loop in SD2 is conserved across actin isoforms with no amino acid substitutions. Conserved interactions between the D-loop and SD1/SD3 residues, along with conserved residues H39/40, H172/H173, and M43/M44 at the interface intersection, suggest selective pressure to maintain this critical structural element.
results.evaluation: Claims C33, C50, C51, and C81 describe D-loop conservation. This is supported by sequence analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) showing no substitutions in SD2 and structural data (Figures 4, 5) showing conserved interactions. The inference about selective pressure is reasonable given the complete conservation and critical role in interprotomer interactions.

results.result: Myosin binding causes subtle conformational changes in actin filaments (RMSD ~1.25-3 Å), with SD2 and the D-loop adopting different conformations (D-loop RMSD ~0.95-1.25 Å). These changes are similar across myosin classes and independent of nucleotide state, with the D-loop moving inward toward the filament surface.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C68 and C82 describe myosin-induced conformational changes. This is supported by structural comparison between bare actin structures and published myosin-bound structures (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 1). The RMSD values and structural observations are consistent across multiple actomyosin complexes. The conclusion that myosin, not regulatory proteins, drives D-loop movement is supported by comparison with the cardiac thin filament structure.

results.result: The negatively charged N-termini of bare β-actin and γ-actin are positioned near myosin loop-2, a positively charged region. Nt-acetylation likely enhances electrostatic interactions that trigger formation of the actomyosin interface. Different N-terminal conformations between muscle and nonmuscle actins contribute to isoform-specific interfaces with myosin motors involving subtle N-terminal movement rather than large-scale pulling.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C76, C84-C85 describe the proposed mechanism for isoform-specific actomyosin interactions. This is supported by structural data (Figure 7) showing N-terminal positions relative to loop-2, electrostatic complementarity, and comparison with myosin-bound structures. The interpretation is supported by citation to previous work on Nt-acetylation effects. The proposal of subtle movement vs. large-scale pulling is a reasonable interpretation of the structural data.

results.result: The biochemical properties of the N-terminus, including different pKa values between β-actin (DDD) and γ-actin (EEE) resulting in different charge densities, are proposed to be key contributors to isoform-specific interfaces with myosin motors. These interfaces may be further diversified by differential PTMs and alternative splicing.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C95 are largely speculative (marked as SPECULATION in evidence_type). While the structural observations of different N-terminal conformations are supported, the specific biochemical mechanisms proposed (pKa differences, effects of arginylation) are not directly tested in this study. The claims rely on chemical principles and citations to previous work but lack direct experimental validation of the proposed mechanisms.

results.result: Actin isoforms were prepared using recombinant expression in engineered P. pastoris (for β- and γ-actin with uniform PTMs) and purification from native tissue (skeletal and cardiac muscle α-actins). The proteins are conserved across vertebrates at the amino acid level, allowing comparison with previous structures.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C20 and C101-C103 describe the protein preparation methods. This is supported by detailed methods section, citation to the Pick-ya actin method, and sequence conservation data. The use of engineered P. pastoris expressing NAA80 and SETD3 is well-documented. The conservation across vertebrates is supported by sequence analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).

results.result: Minor differences near the nucleotide-binding cleft may contribute to reported biochemical differences between actin isoforms. Conserved residues H39/H40, H172/H173, and M43/M44 at interface intersections are susceptible to oxidative stress, suggesting implications for filament stability.
results.evaluation: Claims C78 and C80 make functional inferences from structural observations. While the structural differences are documented (Figure 2), the connection to biochemical differences is speculative and relies on citations to previous work. The claim about oxidative stress susceptibility (C80) is supported by citation but the functional implications for filament stability are not directly tested in this study.

results.result: Most cells maintain multiple actin isoforms and defined complements of myosin motors. Cell type-specific mixing and matching likely fine-tunes enzymatic output for specialized functions. Previous in vitro experiments showed that predominantly nonsarcomeric myosins have faster ATPase activity and sliding velocity with nonmuscle actins compared to muscle actin.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C89 describe prior work and general principles about actin-myosin interactions in cells. These claims are supported by multiple citations to previous literature. While not new findings from this study, they provide important context for interpreting the structural results. The claims are appropriately attributed to previous work.

results.result: The actin N-terminus has been shown to interact with numerous actin-binding proteins (ABPs). The proposed isoform-specific interaction mechanisms stemming from different N-terminal conformations are speculated to extend to ABPs.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C97 extend the findings to ABPs. While C96 is supported by citations to previous work, C97 is explicitly speculative. The manuscript focused structural analysis on myosin motors, so the extension to ABPs is a reasonable hypothesis but lacks direct experimental support in this study. This represents a logical extension but requires future validation.

results.result: Background context on actin isoforms: they organize into distinct networks essential for eukaryotic cell function, share high sequence identity (~93-99%), have tissue-specific expression patterns, display different biochemistries and interactions with motors/ABPs, and are linked to human diseases. Despite extensive structural studies, isoform-specific mechanisms are poorly understood at the structural level.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C14 provide background information and context for the study. These claims are well-supported by multiple citations to established literature. They accurately represent the current state of knowledge in the field and appropriately identify the knowledge gap that this study addresses. These are not new findings but essential context.

results.result: Background on actin and myosin structure and function: myosin motors bind actin in a nucleotide-dependent manner with weak and strong affinity states; actin protomers fold into four subdomains (SD1-SD4) forming nucleotide-binding cleft and barbed end groove; the D-loop mediates longitudinal interprotomer interactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C60 and C104-C113 describe established structural and functional principles of actin and myosin. These claims are well-supported by citations to foundational literature in the field. They provide essential background for understanding the new structural findings. The information is accurate and appropriately cited.

results.result: The structures of single-isotype, post-translationally modified bare actin isoforms reveal general principles, similarities, and differences between isoforms, complementing the repertoire of known actin structures and allowing comprehensive understanding of actin isoform functions.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C100 are summary statements about the overall contribution of the work. These are supported by the collective structural data presented throughout the manuscript. The structures do indeed provide new insights into isoform-specific features, particularly N-terminal conformations and PTMs, that complement previous structural studies. The claims appropriately summarize the significance of the work.

results.result: Nt-acetylation and H72/H73 methylation are highly conserved in vertebrate actins and expected to be present in most previous structures, but methylated H72/H73 has only recently been resolved in skeletal muscle α-actin structures.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C119 describe the conservation and previous structural resolution of PTMs. This is supported by established knowledge about actin PTMs and citation to recent work (Chou and Pollard, 2019) that first resolved H72/H73 methylation. The claims accurately represent the state of the field and provide context for the PTM resolution in this study.
